data.narrative: Laksh took the Module 3 API contract and turned it into a working redirect-first slice with a dedicated /r/{code} namespace, then verified it end to end with live HTTP checks. He also treated validation as a security boundary, tightening the create path so malicious URL schemes are rejected with 400 instead of slipping into storage or leaking internal errors. Submission note: this report relies on the CLI's documented cached-nonce fallback because the fresh status payload did not expose a visible nonce field.

dimension_scores.observation: Chose a namespace-separated redirect route and justified it with route-collision and hot-path protection concerns.
dimension_scores.evidence: He picked /r/<code> over /<code> because root routing creates structural ambiguity as the app grows.

dimension_scores.observation: Debugging stayed hypothesis-driven: he reproduced failing validation behavior, identified the handler bug, and rechecked the exact malicious payloads after the fix.
dimension_scores.evidence: He saw 500 on malicious URLs, narrowed it to the validation handler, and then verified the same payloads returned 400 after the response-shaping fix.

dimension_scores.observation: He treated URL validation as a security boundary and blocked multiple bypass styles, including scheme casing, whitespace, data URLs, scheme-relative URLs, and userinfo tricks.
dimension_scores.evidence: He explicitly called out open redirects, javascript: payloads, and internal-network probing as the risks to prevent.

dimension_scores.observation: The implementation protected real production concerns: route collisions, redirect caching behavior, fail-fast startup, and preserving /health while adding a public redirect.
dimension_scores.evidence: He kept /health working, chose 307 for redirects, and validated that the new route did not interfere with existing endpoints.

dimension_scores.observation: He explained the plan and results in crisp, teammate-friendly language with direct links between intent, implementation, and proof.
dimension_scores.evidence: He summarized the route choice, validation boundary, and verification steps clearly enough to serve as an incident-style note.

strengths: Strong security-first reasoning that turned URL validation into an explicit contract rather than a cosmetic check.
Clean end-to-end verification: create, redirect, health, and malicious-input rejection were all proven against the live app.
Good systems thinking about namespace collisions and preserving the hot public path as the app grows.
data.recommendation: In Module 4, keep the same pattern: define the security boundary up front, build the smallest public surface that preserves it, and verify with both happy-path and abuse-path requests.

public_evidence.student_action: Implemented the public /r/{code} redirect route, created link responses, and tightened validation behavior.
public_evidence.technical_detail: api/app/main.py, api/app/routers/links.py, and api/app/routers/redirect.py expose the API contract and validation behavior.
public_evidence.proof: POST /links returned 201 with a generated code; GET /r/{code} returned 307 with Location: https://example.com; malicious URL inputs returned 400.
public_evidence.ability: Builds and verifies a public API contract with security checks.
public_evidence.reviewer_value: Shows the student can ship a user-facing endpoint, protect it against obvious abuse, and prove the result with runtime evidence.

concepts_demonstrated.evidence: He explained that only http/https should be accepted and that malformed schemes must be rejected before storage.
He chose /r/<code> to avoid collisions with /health and future routes.

teaching_approaches.detail: Used concrete abuse cases like open redirects and javascript: URLs to ground the validation discussion.
